'''Michael D. Atkinson''' is a mathematician and computer scientist known for his work in the theory of [[permutation patterns]] and for contributions to algorithm design, data structures, and algebra. He is an emeritus professor at the [[University of Otago]].

== Education and career ==
Atkinson earned his B.A. (1967) and D.Phil. (1970) in mathematics from the [[University of Oxford]], where he was a member of [[The Queen's College, Oxford|The Queen's College]] and a student of [[Peter M. Neumann]].<ref name=phd>{{MathGenealogy|id=46090}}</ref> His doctoral work focused on varieties of groups, within the area of [[group theory]].

He taught at [[Cardiff University|University College, Cardiff]] from 1970 to 1982, then joined the [[Carleton University]] School of Computer Science in Canada, where he became a full professor in 1983. In 1992, Atkinson moved to the [[University of St Andrews]] as Professor of Algorithms and head of the School of Mathematical and Computational Sciences (1994–1997). He joined the University of Otago in 2000 and retired in 2012.<ref>{{cite web |last=Atkinson |first=Mike |title=Brief career history |url=https://www.cs.otago.ac.nz/staffpriv/mike/HomePages/career.html |access-date=2025-05-28 |website=www.cs.otago.ac.nz}}</ref>

== Research ==
Atkinson's early research spanned algebra, permutation groups, bilinear complexity, and algorithmic linear algebra. His 1975 paper on block-finding algorithms for permutation groups<ref>{{cite journal |last=Atkinson |first=M. D. |title=An algorithm for finding the blocks of a permutation group |journal=Mathematics of Computation |volume=29 |issue=131 |year=1975 |pages=911–913 |doi=10.2307/2005304|jstor=2005304 }}</ref> gave the first polynomial-time algorithm for the problem.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Luks |first=Eugene M. |date=1987-03-01 |title=Computing the composition factors of a permutation group in polynomial time |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02579204 |journal=Combinatorica |language=en |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=89 |doi=10.1007/BF02579204 |issn=1439-6912}}</ref> He later made contributions to data structures and computational geometry, notably on [[min-max heap]]s,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Atkinson |first1=M. D. |last2=Sack |first2=J.-R.|author2-link=Jörg-Rüdiger Sack |last3=Santoro |first3=N. |last4=Strothotte |first4=T. |title=Min-max heaps and generalized priority queues |journal=Communications of the ACM |volume=29 |issue=10 |year=1986 |pages=996–1000 |doi=10.1145/6617.6621}}</ref> geometric congruence testing,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Atkinson |first=M. D. |title=An optimal algorithm for geometrical congruence |journal=Journal of Algorithms |volume=8 |issue=2 |year=1987 |pages=159–172 |doi=10.1016/0196-6774(87)90036-8}}</ref> the cyclic [[Tower of Hanoi|Towers of Hanoi]],<ref>{{cite journal |last=Atkinson |first=M. D. |title=The cyclic towers of Hanoi |journal=Information Processing Letters |volume=13 |issue=3 |year=1981 |pages=118–119 |doi=10.1016/0020-0190(81)90123-X}}</ref> and frequency assignment problems in communication networks.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Atkinson |first1=M. D. |last2=Santoro |first2=N. |last3=Urrutia |first3=J. |title=Integer sets with distinct sums and differences and carrier frequency assignments for nonlinear repeaters |journal=IEEE Transactions on Communications |volume=34 |issue=6 |year=1986 |pages=614–617 |doi=10.1109/TCOM.1986.1096587}}</ref>

In the late 1990s, Atkinson shifted his research to permutation patterns.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Atkinson |first=Mike |title=A life in mathematics |url=https://www.cs.otago.ac.nz/staffpriv/mike/HomePages/Life-in-Maths.html |access-date=2025-05-28 |website=www.cs.otago.ac.nz}}</ref> His 1999 paper ''Restricted permutations''<ref>{{cite journal |last=Atkinson |first=M. D. |title=Restricted permutations |journal=Discrete Mathematics |volume=195 |issue=1–3 |year=1999 |pages=27–38 |doi=10.1016/S0012-365X(98)00306-0|doi-broken-date=4 July 2025 }}</ref> has been described as "foundational" in the field.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brignall |first=Robert |date=2024-04-19 |title=Labelled well-quasi-order in juxtapositions of permutation classes |url=https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/view/v31i2p21 |journal=The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics |volume=31 |issue=2 |page=2 |doi=10.37236/12655 |issn=1077-8926}}</ref> In 2003, he co-founded the [[Permutation Patterns (conference)|Permutation Patterns]] conference with [[Michael H. Albert]], which has played a central role in the development of the field.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bassino |first1=Frédérique |last2=Bouvel |first2=Mathilde |last3=Rossin |first3=Dominique |date=2015-03-20 |title=A foreword by the guest editors |url=https://intlpress.com/JDetail/1806626669047816194 |journal=Journal of Combinatorics |language=EN |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=1–2 |issn=2150-959X}}</ref> Their 2005 joint paper ''Simple permutations and pattern restricted permutations''<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Albert |first1=M. H. |author1-link=Michael H. Albert|last2=Atkinson |first2=M. D. |title=Simple permutations and pattern restricted permutations |journal=Discrete Mathematics |volume=300 |issue=1–3 |year=2005 |pages=1–15 |doi=10.1016/j.disc.2004.12.013|doi-broken-date=4 July 2025 }}</ref> introduced structural decomposition techniques, now known as the substitution decomposition. This work, described as "formative",<ref>{{Cite book |last=Vatter |first=Vincent |chapter=Permutation classes |publisher=CRC Press |year=2015 |isbn=978-1-4822-2085-8 |title=Handbook of Enumerative Combinatorics |editor-last=Bóna |editor-first=Miklós |editor-link=Miklós Bóna |location=Boca Raton, Florida |pages=793 |doi=10.1201/b18255}}</ref> refined the analysis begun in his earlier work with Tim Stitt on the wreath product.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Atkinson |first1=M. D. |last2=Stitt |first2=T. |title=Restricted permutations and the wreath product |journal=Discrete Mathematics |volume=259 |issue=1–3 |year=2002 |pages=19–36 |doi=10.1016/S0012-365X(02)00443-0}}</ref> Together with Albert and [[Martin Klazar]], Atkinson also enumerated the simple permutations that arise in this decomposition.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Albert |first1=M. H. |author1-link=Michael H. Albert|last2=Atkinson |first2=M. D. |last3=Klazar |first3=Martin | author3-link = Martin Klazar |title=The enumeration of simple permutations |journal=Journal of Integer Sequences |volume=6 |issue=4 |year=2003 |pages=Article 03.4.4 |url=https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL6/Albert/albert.html}}</ref> In later work, he and co-authors introduced the notion of geometric grid classes,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Albert |first1=M. H. |author1-link=Michael H. Albert|last2=Atkinson |first2=M. D. |last3=Bouvel |first3=M. |last4=Ruškuc |first4=N. |last5=Vatter |first5=V. |title=Geometric grid classes of permutations |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=365 |issue=11 |year=2013 |pages=5859–5881 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-2013-05804-7}}</ref> another tool in the study of the structure of permutation classes.
